The Pro series of GPT models continues to be really impressive for one-shot problems that involve complex calculations, references, or sophisticated ideas.

It isn't particularly fast (or particularly pleasant) but GPT-6 Pro gives that "ask one question of the great oracle" feel.

Less than three years ago, GPT-4 was the best model in the world, as it had been for a year, and we were all speculating whether there was some unique secret method that OpenAI had or whether GPT-4 was just as good as LLMs would ever get.

(The answer to both questions was "no")

GPT-4 could do 4 minutes of independent work with a 50% chance of success.

Current models can do multiple weeks of work, and January 2026 is a reasonable cut-off for the moment agentic work started.

Large productivity impacts before that would mostly be confined to coding.

quoted_tweet.text: Steve was very early on this. But he’s exactly right—chatbot era was never going to be a huge productivity boost. Analyses should put the line at January 2026; agentic AI is where productivity gains are.

Your PDF parser guesses at tables.

LlamaIndex published the Document Parsing Protocol, a working draft with 140 rules for what a correct parse looks like across text, tables, forms, charts and diagrams. Two parsers can capture every word on a page and still hand your agent outputs that mean different things.

Their example is a sales table with years across the top and quarters underneath. Ask for Q2 2024. One parser pushed the quarters into the body, so the agent has to guess the year. Another dropped the years, so Q2 matches two columns. A third got the right number by inventing a label the page never printed.

the default that costs you: checking that the words came through and calling it done. The text looks fine, and the meaning went missing.

how to test yours this week:

1. Take your messiest real page, with merged headers or a split table.
2. Get the Claude skill or the ChatGPT reference file from parseprotocol .com.
3. Attach the page image and paste the prompt from the site.
4. Compare that output with what your current parser produced.

the check: ask a question that depends on the header, like one quarter of one year. If the answer needs a guess, your pipeline is guessing in production too.

Charts are the hardest part, since the values only exist as pixels. I use a prompt that crops and reads them step by step, and reports each table value with a confidence level.

DPP 0.1 is open for feedback on GitHub.

the protocol:
https://www.parseprotocol.com

the chart reading prompt:
https://godofprompt.ai/prompt-library/dense-chart-reading-with-a-crop-tool

text:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://hackertube.org/

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.
